# Forge Non-Greenfield Build Modes — Overview (FEAT-FORGE-008)

## What Forge does today

Forge is our fleet-based autonomous build orchestrator. It takes a queued build off the work queue and drives it through a chain of GuardKit slash-command stages — specify, plan, build, review, work — each executed as a sandboxed subprocess. Every stage passes through a confidence checkpoint that can auto-approve it, flag it for human review, or hard-stop the build, with approval requests routed back to the operator over an approval channel. Forge records durable stage history, recovers from crashes, and accepts CLI steering (cancel, skip) mid-run.

## The gap

Only one mode exists today: a full greenfield run (Mode A) that performs upfront product-discovery and architecture stages before building each feature in a design catalogue. That is heavy for everyday work on projects that already exist.

## What the operator wants

Two lighter, non-greenfield modes that sit alongside Mode A as first-class citizens:

- **Mode B (Feature)** — add a single new feature to an existing project, without re-running the upfront product-discovery and architecture work; the project's current architecture and design baseline are taken as given.
- **Mode C (Review-Fix)** — run a review-then-fix loop over an existing subject, turning the issues a review raises into fix work.

Each mode should reuse the existing orchestration substrate rather than fork it, and each should land in a sensible terminal outcome.

# FEAT-FORGE-008 — Constraints & Operating Rules

## Build on the existing substrate

The new modes must not fork the orchestration core. Mode B and Mode C are expected to ride on the same machinery Mode A already uses:

- the confidence-gated **checkpoint** (auto-approve / flag-for-review / hard-stop);
- the operator **approval channel** and its request/response round-trip;
- **durable stage history** as the authoritative record of what a build has done;
- **CLI steering** — cancel and skip — accepted while a build is running;
- **correlation identifiers** threaded from the queue through to the build's terminal state.

## Constitutional rule

Pull-request review is pinned to mandatory human approval: no upstream confidence score or calibration prior may auto-approve a pull request. This rule is mode-agnostic and must hold in any mode we add, enforced at both the prompt and executor layers.

## Resilience & concurrency

A build that crashes part-way through must recover from its recorded history rather than from any in-flight subprocess. Several builds may be active at once — potentially in different modes — and each must keep an isolated approval channel and stage chain so responses never cross between builds.

## Steering & idempotency

Cancel and skip must behave sensibly per stage; some stages should refuse a skip outright. Duplicate or replayed approval responses must not corrupt a build's recorded outcome.

# FEAT-FORGE-008 — Integration & Context Notes

## The stage palette

The stages Forge sequences are GuardKit slash commands. Mode A wires up the full set, from product discovery and architecture through per-feature specification, planning, building, review, and fix work. The two new modes are expected to draw on a subset of the same commands rather than introduce new ones — Mode B working from an existing project's baseline at the feature level, Mode C driven by an initial review of an existing subject and the fix work that review implies.

## Responsive supervisor

The long build and work stages should run asynchronously so the supervisor stays responsive and can sequence other queued builds while one build's slow stage is in flight. Each subprocess stays confined to its allotted worktree and must not reach outside it.

## History that reads true to the mode

A non-greenfield build's stage history should reflect only what that mode actually ran — a Mode B history should not carry product-discovery or architecture entries for stages it never executed, and a Mode C history should show the review preceding the fix work, with each fix attributable to the issue that prompted it.

## Prior art

These modes are adaptations of the existing greenfield capstone: same async dispatch shape, same constitutional review pin, same per-artefact attribution conventions — reshaped into a shorter feature chain and a cyclic review-fix chain.

# FEAT-JARVIS-005 — Build Queue Dispatch to Forge: Overview

## Context
Jarvis is our terminal-based supervisor agent. Rich chats with it in a loop, and one of the things it can do is hand a planned feature off to Forge, the downstream automated build pipeline. Today that hand-off is only a stub: the queue-build capability logs a line and returns. We want to close the loop for real.

## What we want
When Rich asks Jarvis to queue a planned feature, Jarvis should publish a genuine build-queued message onto our messaging transport and hand control straight back to the chat loop. The supervisor's next turn must never block on the build pipeline.

Jarvis should confirm the message actually landed on the transport before it tells Rich the build is queued, and it should degrade gracefully when that confirmation is slow to arrive.

Forge then builds asynchronously and emits stage-complete events as each stage finishes. Jarvis should subscribe to those events, match each one back to the chat session that queued the build, and surface progress to Rich as short status lines shown between prompts — never injected mid-reply. Every dispatch should leave a trace in routing history.

# FEAT-JARVIS-005 — Constraints and Operating Realities

## Non-functional expectations
- **Never block the supervisor.** Queuing a build must return control to the chat loop immediately; the next turn cannot wait on Forge.
- **Confirm before claiming.** Jarvis reports "queued" only once the transport confirms receipt, and must stay responsive if that confirmation is slow to come back.
- **Progress between prompts.** Status updates are shown between prompts, never in the middle of a reply.

## Realities we must survive
- The messaging transport, or the routing-history substrate, can be down when a dispatch is attempted.
- Jarvis and Forge restart independently; either may be mid-cycle when the other comes or goes.
- Multiple chat sessions run at once. A build queued in one session must never surface its notifications in another.
- Stage-complete events can arrive faster than Rich reads them; the backlog held for a session cannot grow without bound.
- Malformed or spoofed events can arrive on the subscription and must not corrupt state or mislead Rich.
- Shutdown must not hang waiting on an unresponsive broker.
- Build dispatch draws on the same bounded concurrency pool as specialist-dispatch; the two compete for the same slots.

# FEAT-JARVIS-005 — Integration Context

## Transport
Dispatch and notifications both ride our NATS JetStream transport. Jarvis publishes build-queued messages; Forge consumes them and, as it works, publishes stage-complete events on a related subject that Jarvis subscribes to. This is a one-way, fire-and-forget hand-off: Jarvis does not wait for Forge to consume the work — it returns as soon as the transport acknowledges the publish.

## Correlation
Each queued build carries an identifier so that when a stage-complete event comes back, Jarvis can match it to the originating session and show the update to the right person, on the interface that session is using. Jarvis keeps an in-memory map of in-flight builds to do this matching. Over a long-running supervisor, that map cannot be allowed to grow unbounded, and the same explicit identifier could in principle be reused across two queue requests.

## Routing history
Every build-queue dispatch is recorded in Jarvis's routing-history trace, and matched stage-complete events should attach to that same record so the history of a build is auditable. That substrate, too, can be unavailable at the moment of dispatch.

# Fleet Registration & Specialist Dispatch — Overview

## Where we are

Jarvis is our general-purpose supervisor agent. Today it can reason about *which* specialist should handle a request, but it can't actually hand work off — the fleet is a hard-coded stub and there is no transport behind the routing seam. This phase makes Jarvis a real citizen of the agent fleet. The reasoning model's tool surface is unchanged; only the transport behind the seam swaps.

## What this phase delivers

On startup Jarvis should announce itself to the fleet so other agents can see it and know it is alive, then keep that liveness fresh by re-announcing on an interval. It should discover the specialists currently on the fleet — architect, product owner, and others — from the live shared capability catalogue rather than the stub, and refresh that view as fleet membership changes.

With a specialist chosen, Jarvis round-trips real work over our NATS message bus: it sends a command on the specialist's command subject, waits for the matching reply on that specialist's result subject, and returns the specialist's output to the original caller. Command and result subjects are keyed per agent. Dispatch is a request/reply interaction, not fire-and-forget — the caller gets the specialist's actual result back.

# Fleet Dispatch — Constraints & Resilience

## Bounded, timed dispatch

Every dispatch must be time-bounded: if the chosen specialist does not reply within the dispatch window, the attempt is abandoned. Callers may request a shorter or longer window, but only within a supported range — a request outside the range is rejected at the tool boundary rather than silently clamped. The reply-wait budget applies per attempt.

## Redirect, then degrade

When a specialist times out or reports an error, Jarvis should redirect the work to an alternative capable specialist rather than failing outright. Redirection is bounded — once the retry budget is exhausted the dispatch degrades cleanly with an explicit unresolved outcome. Candidate resolution must be deterministic, so a given fleet state always selects the same specialist and the decision replays identically across runs.

## Shared concurrency pool

Dispatch draws on a bounded in-flight concurrency pool shared with the other dispatch paths in the same supervisor process. When the pool is saturated a further dispatch is rejected synchronously as overloaded — wait and retry — rather than queued without limit. The slot must be released on every dispatch outcome, success or failure.

## Soft-fail

If NATS or the knowledge graph is unavailable — at startup or mid-session — Jarvis must not crash; it falls back to a usable state and stays a useful chat surface. On shutdown it drains in-flight dispatches and deregisters from the fleet within a bounded window.

# Routing History & Message-Bus Conventions

## Decision traces

This phase produces the first live writes to Jarvis's routing history (per ADR-FLEET-001). Each dispatch decision is recorded as a trace-rich record: which specialist was chosen, that specialist's reported status at decision time, the per-attempt outcomes, and a reference to any sub-agent trace. These writes are best-effort — a failure to persist history must not fail the dispatch itself, only log a warning.

## Large traces and sensitive content

A trace record that exceeds the inline size budget is offloaded to a per-decision file on the local filesystem under the traces directory; smaller records stay inline. Each decision maps to a single trace-file path, so a write against an already-present path is a collision that must be handled explicitly rather than blindly overwritten. Before any record is persisted — inline or offloaded — sensitive material must be redacted at the write boundary.

## Bus conventions

Subjects follow a singular topic convention (no plural forms). Every envelope Jarvis emits carries an audit field identifying Jarvis as the source. A specialist reply that arrives after its attempt's wait budget has elapsed is treated as late and discarded at the transport layer — the outcome stands as a timeout, not a delayed success.

# Architect Ingestion v2 — Overview (FEAT-RAG-08)

## Why

The architect agent answers design questions by retrieving over a knowledge index. Today that index is built from a single `knowledge.jsonl` file ingested into a vector collection. We want the architect to also draw on architecture books that arrive as Docling-derived markdown (produced upstream from source PDFs), so a newly added or refreshed book can land in the same index without a detour through the agentic-dataset-factory pipeline.

## Outcome we want

After this change, an operator can point the ingestion at a markdown book and have its content become retrievable alongside the existing JSONL-sourced entries — one index, both origins, retrieval spanning both. Re-adding the same book must not multiply its content in the collection: the pipeline should be idempotent and safe to re-run, and it should report what it actually ingested — what was added and what was skipped — so the operator can trust the result. The architect corpus is homogeneous — one kind of source — so we are not introducing source-type folders or taxonomies; origin just needs to stay distinguishable enough to reason about later.

# Architect Ingestion v2 — Constraints & Non-Functionals

## Embedding path

Alongside the new markdown path, the architect's embedding calls move off the direct Ollama embeddings endpoint and onto the fleet-canonical, OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint used across the rest of the fleet — for both ingestion and retrieval-time query embedding. This removes a standing fleet-policy violation. The endpoint must sit inside the fleet's trust boundary; ingestion should refuse an embedding endpoint that points outside it rather than silently reaching an off-fleet host.

## Model consistency

A collection is embedded with a particular model. Re-ingesting with a differently-named embedding model must not silently corrupt the collection's queryability; ingestion should notice a mismatch between the configured model and what the collection was built with and refuse rather than proceed. Note the deployed model may be registered under a shorter alias than its upstream identifier.

## Concurrency & failure

Retrieval that happens while an ingestion is in flight must see a consistent view, not a half-written mix. Two ingestion runs against the same store at once should fail clearly rather than surface a raw database lock error. If the embedding service returns an error partway through a batch, the run must abort without leaving partial in-flight writes, so a re-run recovers cleanly.

# Architect Ingestion v2 — Integration & Context

## What exists

Ingestion today reads `knowledge.jsonl`, chunks and embeds each entry, and writes it into a persistent vector store with a stable per-chunk identity so the same source content resolves to the same record on re-run. The new markdown path must slot into this same store and reuse the same de-duplication idea: re-ingesting an unchanged source should resolve in place, not append duplicates.

## Markdown specifics

Docling emits one markdown file per book from a source PDF. Each file needs to be split into retrievable chunks, embedded, and stored beside the existing entries. Every chunk must carry the same canonical per-file metadata the existing entries already carry, so downstream retrieval and citation behave uniformly. How that per-file metadata is supplied, what its defaults are, and the exact chunking granularity are all left to design.

## Deliberately out of the neighbouring project

We are borrowing the study-tutor project's ingestion shape but NOT its in-copyright deny-list, its four-folder source-type taxonomy, or its per-chunk citation-anchor inferer — the architect's citations are coarse (`[book: topic]`) and its corpus is homogeneous, so those do not apply here.

# Student Model — Overview

## Why

Study-tutor is our GCSE tutoring agent. Today it has no memory of a learner between sessions: every conversation starts cold. We want the tutor to build and maintain a per-student model in a knowledge graph so it can teach the way a good human tutor does — remembering what a student has covered, how they are doing, and what to come back to.

## What we want

The model should hold a learner profile: who the student is, which subjects and set texts they are studying, the topics and assessment objectives within those, any misconceptions we have observed, and a confidence level per topic. As a student works through tutoring sessions, the tutor should update that confidence per topic, record that a session happened, and note misconceptions as they surface.

On the query side the tutor needs three things: read a student's current state, recommend a small set of topics to study next (prioritising weaker areas), and record a completed session. Recommendations should lean toward topics the student is weak on and topics that are due to be revisited, and should avoid re-recommending something they have only just worked on. Confidence should be expressible in human terms — struggling, developing, secure, mastered — rather than as a raw number.

# Student Model — Constraints and Non-Functionals

## Latency

The caller-facing path is the live tutoring loop, so reads must be fast — the tutor should pull a learner's state without the student waiting. Writes are different: persisting a session or a confidence update can be slower, and the session-end handler must return promptly to the caller regardless of how long the graph takes. So writes should be fire-and-forget — kicked off in the background at every write point, never blocking the tutor's reply.

## Graceful degradation

The student model must not become a single point of failure. If the knowledge graph is briefly unavailable, a read should degrade gracefully rather than error — the tutor falls back to an empty or partial profile and carries on. A background write that fails should be logged, not surfaced to the student. If the graph library is not even installed, the module should still load so the rest of the tutor runs.

## Freshness and durability

Stored facts can go stale; older facts should be flagged as such when read back so the tutor does not over-trust them. At process shutdown, in-flight background writes should be given a bounded chance to finish before the process exits, with anything unfinished logged. Reads are not required to reflect a write that was issued moments earlier.

# Student Model — Scoping, Integration and Seeding

## Isolation

Each learner's data must be strictly scoped so one student can never read another's state. Data is partitioned by group identifiers along the lines of the individual student, the subject, and the whole fleet of learners. The exact naming convention for these group identifiers still needs pinning down — an existing specialist-agent in a sister repo already uses a group-id scheme, and study-tutor should follow our own scope document's convention where the two diverge, but the divergence must be recorded so a future shared-identifier feature can resolve it.

## External services

Writing to the graph involves an extraction step that calls out to a language model to turn session content into structured facts, plus an embeddings endpoint for search. Both are integration boundaries that can be slow or unavailable, and the fire-and-forget write path must tolerate that without affecting the tutor.

## Seeding

We need a one-off seeding script to load an initial cohort of learners and their subjects, texts and topics into the graph. Seeding must be idempotent — running it twice should not duplicate a learner. If the graph store is unreachable when seeding runs, it should defer cleanly rather than half-populate. Seeding an unknown learner should be handled explicitly.

# Primary-Text RAG and Source-Typed Quote Verifier — Overview

## Goal
Study-tutor must quote primary literary texts (novels, plays) accurately when helping students prepare for GCSE English. Today the tutor sometimes emits quotations that do not appear in the source, or presents phrasing lifted from study guides as if it were the author's own words. This feature makes primary-text quotation trustworthy.

## What we want
A retrieval-augmented layer that, each turn, pulls the passages most relevant to the student's question from a source-typed corpus, plus a verifier that inspects any quotation the tutor emits and checks it against the primary text.

The corpus is organised by source type — primary text, secondary study guide, secondary critical writing, historical context — with the source type inferred at ingestion from where a document sits. Retrieval should be able to prefer or filter by source type.

Retrieval is not always wanted: when the session's text has no primary edition available, or the question targets certain kinds of context, the tutor should be able to skip retrieval and reason from what it already knows.

## Verifier outcomes
The verifier classifies each quoted span into one of a few outcomes: a verbatim primary-text match, annotated with its citation; phrasing found only in secondary material, re-expressed as attributed paraphrase; a near-match, gently corrected to the true wording; and a quotation with no traceable source, removed.

# Constraints, Safety, and Resilience

## Copyright
The corpus must stay clean of material we are not licensed to hold. AQA assessment material (past papers, mark schemes, examiner reports and the like) must be refused when someone tries to ingest it, and must never surface in retrieval results even if it slips in. In-copyright modern set texts must not live in the primary-text collection — only public-domain primary works belong there, drawn from canonical editions. The exact refusal mechanism, and the list of titles to block, are for the team to decide.

## Never mislead about attribution
Several invariants must always hold, regardless of retrieval quality. Secondary phrasing must never be returned as the author's own words. A quotation that actually belongs to a different text than the one the session is on must never be annotated against the current text's citation. Overly long verbatim passages must be reduced to a short embedded quotation rather than reproduced wholesale — how long is "too long", and how short the replacement should be, is open. Minor formatting differences between a quote and the source should be tolerated, but fabricated quotes rejected; the tolerance boundary is not yet fixed.

## Degrade gracefully
The corpus loader must survive corrupted or unreadable files without aborting the whole ingest. Retrieval must still work when the reranker is unavailable. When the embedding service is unavailable or too slow to respond, the turn should fall back to reasoning without retrieval rather than hang — the threshold for "too slow" is not yet fixed.

# Integration and Scope

## Where this sits
The per-turn retrieval decision depends on two upstream signals: the student model knows which primary text the current session is about, and the lesson planner knows which assessment objectives the turn is focused on. Both feed the pre-turn choice of whether to retrieve and, if so, what to prefer.

## Coach handover
The verifier is the seam the Coach's quote-fidelity check consumes downstream. Importantly, once the verifier has rewritten or corrected a response, it is that rewritten response — not the tutor's original — that the Coach evaluates. Verifier metadata describing what it did to each quoted span should travel alongside the response so the Coach can score fidelity rather than re-derive it.

## In and out of scope
In scope: source-typed ingestion, the per-turn retrieve-or-not decision, source-filtered retrieval, and post-hoc quote verification over public-domain primary texts.

Out of scope for this phase: letting students supply their own in-copyright texts to be cached per student; grounding quotations before generation rather than checking them afterwards (this phase stays post-hoc verification only); and any retriever or reranker tuning beyond the baseline we already trust.
